# Linear regression assumptions and differences from ANOVA

## Linear regression

###Shortcomes of anova - Complex designs and missing data can make anova
difficult. - Didide data into groups and see which groups explain the
variation - Categorical variables - Simple designs - Requires normality

------------------------------------------------------------------------

###Linear regression - estimate the effect of different variables and
check if they are different than 0, basically explain how well one or
more variables can explain the data. - Residuals needs to be normal -
Variance is equal (Homoscedasticity) - No multicorinearity - Residuals
are uncorrelated - Continuoues and categorical variables - Pretty much
any design - Extended to any distribution of residuals

GOAL: Find the line that best summarizes a lot of data with minimal
error.

## Loading data.

```{r}
sunflower <- read.csv("./data/16_sunflower.csv")

sunflower
```

## Checking outliers on raw data.

```{r}
hist(sunflower$oil)
plot(sunflower$oil, pch = 20, cex = 1.5)
```

## Creating Linear Regression Model

```{r}
model <- lm(data = sunflower, oil ~ variety)
summary(model)
```

## Checking residuals.

```{r}
hist(residuals(model))
plot(residuals(model), pch = 20, cex = 1.5)
```

After checking residuals, we can see shotgun effect, and also they
appear to be in a normal distribution.

## GVLMA, very useful

```{r}
install.packages("gvlma")
library(gvlma)
```

```{r}
gvlma(model)
```

```{r}
plot(gvlma(model), onepage = FALSE)
```

```{r}
plot(model)
```

## Other graphs to check

```{r}
library(performance)
```

# Balanced vs Unbalanced data.

# Filtering Outliers

```{r}
sunflower2 <- read.csv("./data/16_sunflower.csv")
model2 <- lm(data = sunflower2, oil ~ variety)
sunflower2$resid <- residuals(model2)

sunflower2$oil_filt <- sunflower2$oil
sunflower2$oil_filt[sunflower2$resid>4] = NA

sunflower2
```

In balanced data, order of data in anova and in models doesn't matter, in unbalanced data it does matter.

Sums-of-squares

The total of SS doesn't changes, but whichones goes first in the model gets more SS on the model. (If oil ~ block + variety) <- block will get more.

Linear regression is greedy (it does as much it's possible as faster it's possible)


# Showing off balanced data

```{r}
balanced <- read.csv("./data/16_balanced.csv")
balanced

```

```{r}
model1b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~ variety + block)
summary(model1b)
model2b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~  block + variety)
summary(model2b)
```
Removing to make it unbalanced <- still balanced

```{r}
balanced$yield[balanced$variety == "A51"] = NA

balanced

```
```{r}
model3b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~ variety + block)
summary(model3b)
model4b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~  block + variety)
summary(model4b)
```
Remove to be unbalanced <- not equal

```{r}
balanced$yield[balanced$variety == "C11" & balanced$block == "block4"] = NA

model5b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~ variety + block)
summary(model5b)
model6b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~  block + variety)
summary(model6b)

```
Even though changed only a little, it's reasonable to say that with more complex models we will have more problems with this variation.

The general rule is:
- Blocks first,
- Treatments later.

On type 1 SS, you are looking into only one value of the treatments.

On type 2 SS, basically the model is fit multiple times, each time with a different effect in last place, however, higher-order interactions are ignores, and this can be dangerous if interactions are significant.

On type 3, the idea is simillar to type 2, however it is accounting for all other main effects and interactions.


```{r}
model3b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~ variety + block)
model4b <- aov(data = balanced, yield ~  block + variety)


anova(model1b)
anova(model2b)

library(car)
Anova(model1b, type = 2)
Anova(model2b, type = 2)
```
